analysis.one_liner: Hands every acre of Bureau of Land Management land to the states.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the Senate Energy Committee on July 13, 1995, sent to a subcommittee four days later, and died there when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have offered every piece of federal land managed by the Bureau of Land Management — hundreds of millions of acres, mostly in Western states — to the state where it sits, along with the federal mineral and water rights attached to it. Each state could take all of it or nothing. States would keep honoring existing grazing and energy leases, but mining claims would be judged under state law and claim holders would keep their right to patent (buy) the land under the 1872 Mining Law. The bill would also cap the Bureau of Land Management's yearly budget at $800 million.
analysis.who_benefits: Mining companies and mining claim holders gain the most: their claims would be administered under state law rather than federal law, and they would keep the right to obtain full patents to the land under the 1872 Mining Law, which lets them buy federal land containing minerals at 1872-era prices [S3]. Grazing permit holders and energy developers gain because states take over management of leases and permits while the bill requires states to honor them [S3]. Western states would gain title to the land itself, its water rights, and the revenue from developing or selling it [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary of the Interior must offer every BLM-administered land, mineral right, and associated water right to the state where it lies; a state may accept all of it or reject it, and the transfer takes effect ten years after acceptance [S2] [S3].

States must honor valid existing leases and permits and respect federal rights-of-way, so current grazing and energy operations would continue, but under state rather than federal management [S2] [S3].

The validity and continued existence of mining claims would be determined under state law, and claim holders entitled to patents before the transfer would keep that entitlement — preserving the ability to patent claims under the 1872 Mining Law statutes [S3].
The bill caps what the Bureau of Land Management may spend each year at $800 million and directs the Secretary to prioritize spending on the land transfer itself [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The American public, which collectively owns these lands, would bear the cost: the bill places no restriction on a state selling the land it receives, and once transferred, management decisions about access, grazing, logging, mining, and development would be made by state officials instead of on behalf of all Americans [S3]. Hunters, anglers, hikers, and campers who use BLM land would face whatever access rules each state sets. The bill also requires no federal survey of the land before transfer, leaving boundary questions to the states [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: The public owners of federal lands

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no prohibition on a state selling transferred lands; unlike federal law, which holds these lands in trust for the whole nation, a state could dispose of acreage to private buyers, permanently removing it from public access [S3].

States would inherit the full cost of managing vast, fire-prone, remote landscapes; the bill requires states to honor existing leases and military withdrawals without any federal payment to cover the expense, which could pressure states to sell land or intensify development to raise revenue [S3].

Preserving mining patent rights on transferred land would let claim holders buy land containing public minerals at 1872 Mining Law prices, a fraction of market value, with the sale proceeding under the same statutes as before transfer [S3].
Transferring water rights to states, while preserving existing compacts, treaties, and Indian rights, would still shift federally reserved water associated with the lands into state hands [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters in Western states argued that states could manage nearby land better than a distant federal agency, and the bill did preserve wilderness areas, military uses, and Indian trust mineral interests [S3]. But the core exchange favors concentrated users over the general public: mining claim holders keep 1872-era patent rights, existing extractive leases get state-level treatment, and the one thing the bill never does is forbid a state from selling the land to private buyers [S3]. For a public that owns the land and pays for its management, the costs outweigh the local-control benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which passed it to a subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Craig Thomas introduced the bill on July 13, 1995, joined by six Republican cosponsors [S1] [S4] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S5].
On July 17, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Forests and Public Lands, where the record ends [S5].
The committee never reported the bill, and the full Senate and House never voted on it before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The American public kept its land: because the bill never advanced, the hundreds of millions of acres of BLM land, and the minerals and water attached to them, remained federally owned and managed for all citizens rather than transferred to states under a law with no sale restriction. Mining, grazing, and energy interests lost their chance at state-controlled management.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; extractive users lost out

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists, and no Democrat is listed anywhere in its history [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Mining companies and mining claim holders
industries.note: On transferred lands, mining claim validity would be judged under state law and holders would keep their entitlement to federal patents under the 1872 Mining Law — letting them buy land containing public minerals at 1872-era prices. The public, which owns the minerals, would get a fraction of their value [S3].

States must honor existing grazing leases, and state grazing management has historically been cheaper and lighter-touch than federal management. Cheap-forage gains for ranchers come out of the public's share of the land [S3].

Existing energy leases would be honored and future development of transferred lands and their mineral rights would be permitted by state agencies rather than federal land managers, generally on more favorable terms [S3].

States would receive title to land, water rights, and a new revenue base, but would also inherit management and firefighting costs with no federal payment and no cap on what they could lose. Several states would likely have struggled to absorb the cost [S3].
Businesses built on hunting, fishing, and public-land access would face the risk that states with no sale restriction could dispose of land, shrinking the public base their customers use [S3].
